body:
Why genomic information is useful

The genome is the complete set of genetic information of an organism. Studying human genomes can improve understanding of inherited variation, biological diversity, disease susceptibility and some differences in drug response.

Genomic information may be useful in medical research and in selected clinical situations. However, the discovery of a genetic variation does not automatically establish that it causes disease or that a particular treatment will work.

Genomic findings must be interpreted alongside established scientific evidence and appropriate clinical information.

GenomeIndia and the Indian Biological Data Centre

GenomeIndia is an initiative supported by the Government of India's Department of Biotechnology (DBT) to study genetic variation across India's diverse population groups.

On 9 January 2025, the government announced the release of an Indian genomic dataset involving 10,000 whole-genome samples. A further government statement dated 30 April 2025 reported completion of whole-genome sequencing data from more than 10,000 individuals representing major population groups.

The initiative is linked with the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC), which supports the storage and sharing of biological research data under applicable arrangements.

The figures above refer to the reported project dataset and its status on the stated dates. They should not be interpreted as the number of patients who received clinical diagnosis or treatment through a national precision-medicine service.

Why genetic data requires special care

Genetic information may reveal information about a person's inherited characteristics, disease-related risks or biological relationships. Unlike an ordinary password, inherited genetic information cannot simply be changed when privacy is compromised.

Some genetic information is also relevant to biological relatives. Consequently, disclosure may affect people other than the person who originally supplied the sample.

Important safeguards include:

  • Informed consent: Individuals should receive understandable information about the intended collection, testing and use of their information, subject to applicable law and clinical circumstances.
  • Purpose limitation: Data should be used only for permitted and appropriately explained purposes.
  • Access control: Only authorised persons should have access to information needed for their work.
  • Data security: Technical and organisational measures should reduce the risk of theft, loss or unauthorised disclosure.
  • Responsible sharing: Research benefits should be balanced against privacy, consent and the possibility of identifying individuals from shared data.

Removing a person's name from a dataset reduces direct identification, but genetic information may still carry a risk of re-identification when combined with other information. Therefore, removing names alone does not guarantee complete anonymity.

India's data-protection framework

India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on 14 November 2025, with an implementation framework involving different commencement dates for specified requirements.

These instruments concern the protection and lawful handling of digital personal data. Their existence does not mean that every genetic or medical use of data is automatically permitted. Applicable consent requirements, medical confidentiality, research ethics and other relevant safeguards must also be considered.

Cost and equity in biotechnology

A new medical technology can be scientifically valuable yet inaccessible to many patients. Several barriers affect equitable access:

  • High prices: Biological medicines and some genomic tests can be costly to produce or provide.
  • Laboratory capacity: Advanced diagnostic services may be concentrated in a limited number of institutions.
  • Geographical access: Rural and remote populations may face travel costs and delays.
  • Workforce limitations: Trained healthcare workers are needed to interpret complex results appropriately.
  • Unequal representation: Research datasets that underrepresent particular populations may produce findings that are less useful for those groups.
  • Digital exclusion: Lack of connectivity, digital literacy or access to records can limit the benefits of digital health services.

Measures that may improve access include affordable testing, appropriate public procurement, domestic production, stronger laboratory networks, reliable distribution and responsible sharing of research resources.

The international emphasis on equitable precision medicine

On 22 May 2026, the 79th World Health Assembly endorsed resolution WHA79.8 on precision medicine. It emphasised the need to develop clinical, scientific, regulatory and data-governance capacity while making the benefits of precision medicine more equitable.

The central public-health principle is that new technology should improve actual health outcomes, not merely increase the number of tests available to people who can already afford them.

Connecting the major concepts

Biotechnology can be understood through 4 linked questions. What can be manufactured? Recombinant proteins and monoclonal antibodies provide medicines. How can disease be prevented? Vaccines stimulate protective immunity. What can be detected? Molecular and immunological tests identify selected disease-related targets. How can treatment be chosen more precisely? Biomarkers and pharmacogenomics help inform decisions for particular patients.

These applications are related but not interchangeable. A vaccine is not simply a diagnostic test, a DNA test is not automatically a treatment, and a genetic association is not automatically a reliable medical prediction.

Prelims focus

  • GenomeIndia is supported by the Department of Biotechnology.
  • Government reports in January and April 2025 described a GenomeIndia dataset of approximately 10,000 or more whole genomes.
  • IBDC stands for Indian Biological Data Centre.
  • The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in 2023; associated rules were notified in 2025.
  • The 79th World Health Assembly endorsed resolution WHA79.8 on precision medicine on 22 May 2026.
  • Equitable access depends on cost, infrastructure, trained workers and representative research data.
  • Trap: A genomic research database is not the same as a clinical treatment programme, and removing names does not eliminate every privacy risk.

pictures.alt: Four biotechnology pathways distinguish supplying medicines, generating immunity, detecting targets and guiding treatment, linked by shared quality, safety and access requirements.
pictures.caption: Biotechnology connects medicines, prevention, diagnosis and treatment selection, with safety and access relevant throughout.

title: Genomic Data, Privacy, Affordability and Fair Access to Biotechnology
